summary: TRILL is based on IS-IS, which supports multilevel routing, but extending TRILL to several levels raises new problems, such as distributing multi-destination traffic and handling switch nicknames. This informational document discusses alternatives for solving them.

eli5.summary: A big city is easier to handle if split into neighborhoods. This looks at different ways to split up a large network and still deliver mail to everyone.

subtitle: How to divide TRILL networks into hierarchical levels for better scalability.

tldr.problem: TRILL networks using the IS-IS routing protocol face scaling limits. As a network grows, routing computation load, link state database size, and control traffic all increase. The 16-bit nickname space that identifies TRILL switches becomes a hard limit.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC examines two approaches to multilevel (hierarchical) TRILL: unique-nickname (all switch nicknames are globally unique across the campus) and aggregated-nickname (nicknames are local to areas, and only area nicknames are visible outside). Each approach has tradeoffs in complexity, scalability, and backward compatibility.
tldr.outcome: The RFC recommends a mixed design supporting both approaches. A network can start with simpler unique nicknames and later introduce aggregated-nickname areas as it grows. Aggregated nicknames eliminate the nickname exhaustion problem but require border switches to rewrite nickname fields in packet headers.

today: RFC 8243 is an Informational document that provides design guidance for future TRILL standards work. It was published in September 2017 and has not been superseded. The recommendations remain relevant for operators designing large-scale TRILL networks today.

sections.title: Motivation for Scaling TRILL
sections.content:
TRILL is a bridge routing protocol that uses IS-IS, which was designed with multilevel (hierarchical) support from the start. A multilevel TRILL network divides into "areas" connected by a Level 2 backbone. Level 1 routing happens within an area, Level 2 routing between areas.

Scaling problems include: routing computation load grows with network size; the link state database (LSDB) changes frequently and causes control traffic; topology changes take time to converge; the LSDB itself grows large; the 16-bit nickname space limits the number of switches; and multi-destination traffic (broadcast and multicast) stresses the network. Partitioning into areas can reduce all these pressures by a factor roughly equal to the square root of the network size.
sections.eli5: As a bridge network grows, the computer doing all the routing math has to work harder. Splitting the network into separate areas means each area does less work.

sections.title: Unique and Aggregated Nicknames
sections.content:
In the unique-nickname approach, every TRILL switch in the entire campus has a globally unique 16-bit nickname, whether it is in Level 1 or Level 2. This approach is simpler for border switches (no header rewriting) but uses the nickname space inefficiently.

In the aggregated-nickname approach, each area is assigned one or more nicknames representing the area as a whole. Individual switch nicknames within an area are only locally significant and never appear outside it. Border switches must translate (rewrite) the ingress and/or egress nickname fields in TRILL headers as packets move between levels.

Aggregated nicknames avoid nickname exhaustion, reduce the amount of routing information passed between areas, and simplify Reverse Path Forwarding (RPF) checks. The cost is added complexity in border switches and the need for address learning across area boundaries.
sections.eli5: With unique nicknames, every person in every neighborhood has their own unique ID everywhere. With aggregated nicknames, neighborhoods have IDs, and people inside use local IDs that mean nothing outside.

sections.title: Nickname Allocation and Border Operations
sections.content:
With unique nicknames across areas, each area needs to be allocated a block of nicknames to avoid contention. Using new IS-IS TLVs to announce which nicknames are available (or forbidden) would require updating all switches in an area, which is painful if it means advertising tens of thousands of entries. A better method is a new TLV conveying nickname ranges, but this requires software updates.

Aggregated nicknames eliminate this contention entirely but shift the burden to border switches. In the "border learning" variant, border switches learn MAC addresses from outside their area and must know which far-away nicknames (or area nicknames) to reach. This requires address sharing between border switches, often via ESADI. In the "swap nickname field" variant, border switches maintain and swap separate ingress and egress nickname fields in a TRILL header, but this requires changing the packet format and is impractical in the near term.
sections.eli5: Unique nicknames mean someone at headquarters has to say which numbers are free in each neighborhood. Aggregated nicknames mean each neighborhood controls its own numbers, and the border gateways handle the translation.

sections.title: Multi-Destination Traffic and Tree Handling
sections.content:
Multi-destination packets (broadcast and multicast) are distributed via trees rooted at TRILL switches. In a multilevel network, trees can span multiple areas. With aggregated nicknames, each area can have local trees rooted in the area, and only area-level trees need to be coordinated in Level 2. This avoids the constraint (present in unique-nickname designs) that multi-destination traffic can only split across a restricted set of border switches.

When a unicast packet turns into a multi-destination packet at a border (because the destination is unknown), the RFC discusses marking such packets with a scope indicating "this area only" to avoid flooding back to Level 2. New tree encodings could carry this information in the egress nickname field, but again, these require hardware changes.
sections.eli5: Mail trucks deliver to neighborhoods using different routes. If a package destination is unknown in a neighborhood, the gateway can flood it locally without accidentally sending it back to Level 2.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Mixed Networks
sections.content:
The RFC suggests a pragmatic design: support both unique-nickname and aggregated-nickname areas in the same campus. Switches within an area need not know whether they are in a unique or aggregated area; the border switches determine this. A network can start with all unique-nickname areas (simpler to deploy) and later introduce aggregated areas as it scales.

A challenge is handling old TRILL switches that do not understand multilevel concepts. If multilevel-ignorant switches exist in an area, border switches can elect a single designated border router (DBRB) and route all inter-area traffic through it, sacrificing load splitting for compatibility. Multi-access links with end stations (which are TRILL-unaware) require careful coordination of Appointed Forwarders across area boundaries.
sections.eli5: Old switches don't know about areas, so all cross-area traffic can go through one border gateway until they are upgraded. New areas don't need to wait for old switches to be upgraded everywhere.

sections.title: Area Configuration and Link State Representation
sections.content:
Each area has an area address (currently zero in TRILL, but the RFC proposes non-zero values to prevent accidental merging). Within an area, border routers elect a Designated Border RBridge (DBRB), which acquires area nicknames and generates Level 1 Link State PDUs advertising external information to the area and Level 2 LSPs representing the area. The DBRB can also advertise a pseudonode IS-IS ID for the area, similar to how a Designated Router creates a pseudonode for a link.

If area addresses are configured to be non-zero, the smallest concern is multilevel-ignorant legacy TRILL switches that reject non-zero areas. The RFC suggests several solutions: update all switches, configure borders to remove the area address for old switches, accept accidental merging, or use a new optional TLV for an area name instead of changing the fixed area address field.
sections.eli5: Each neighborhood elects a mayor who tells Level 2 about what's in the neighborhood and listens for news from outside.
